The article titled "[AI-generated is the new fake news](https://globalwitness.org/en/campaigns/digital-threats/ai-generated-is-the-new-fake-news/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=16998328683&gbraid=0AAAAADm6LOCfqDUiM_hyKa2KgnBU4dvk6&gclid=CjwKCAjwyabTBhBFEiwAM3mNUGtJOcONJIpQFB721NkYSwW9uB9rZWget6IsnYKn9vccPdi-DAqYfRoCbogQAvD_BwE)" from Global Witness discusses the growing confusion surrounding AI-generated content, particularly in the context of elections. Here are the key points:

- The article highlights a viral audio deepfake related to the Slovakian election, illustrating the potential for AI-generated content to disrupt democratic processes.
- While AI-generated information has become more prevalent, its impact on actual election results has not been as significant as feared. Concerns remain, especially in the U.S., about the use of AI to produce false information in campaigns.
- The phrase "AI-generated" is increasingly used as a tactic to discredit political opponents, similar to the previous use of "fake news." This tactic can create distrust and confusion in political discourse.
- The article notes that during U.S. election campaigns, there have been instances where genuine images were misattributed as AI-generated, further complicating public perception.

Overall, the article argues that while AI has not yet overwhelmed reliable information, the implications of its misuse in political contexts are concerning.

items.title: "AI-generated" is the new "fake news" | Global Witness
items.summary:
## Content type

[Opinion](https://globalwitness.org/en/opinion/)

## Campaigns

[Digital Threats to Democracy](https://globalwitness.org/en/campaigns/digital-threats/)

## Locations

[North America](https://globalwitness.org/en/regions/north-america/)

[United States](https://globalwitness.org/en/regions/north-america/united-states/)

## Topics

[Big Tech](https://globalwitness.org/en/topics/big-tech/), [Disinformation](https://globalwitness.org/en/topics/disinformation/), [Elections](https://globalwitness.org/en/topics/elections/)

Widespread confusion over AI around the US election is the result of a poorly regulated tech sector

![](https://gw.hacdn.io/media/images/DTD_listing_images_WIP1.width-800.png)

Douglas Rissing / Getty

In 2023, an [audio deepfake](https://www.wired.com/story/slovakias-election-deepfakes-show-ai-is-a-danger-to-democracy/#:~:text=Fact-checkers%20scrambled%20to%20deal%20with%20faked%20audio%20recordings%20released%20days) of a politician talking about rigging the Slovakian election went viral. Many people saw this as the start of a new era of [digital deception](https://globalwitness.org/en/topics/disinformation/), with AI-generated content on course to disrupt elections around the globe.

Now in the last quarter of this ["Year of Elections"](https://globalwitness.org/en/topics/elections/), without a doubt, AI has changed the information landscape. But its effects haven’t been as straightforward as people predicted.

For sure, AI-generated information has proliferated, from [bot farms](https://www.voanews.com/a/russia-falsely-denies-ties-with-ai-operated-disinformation-bot-farm-on-x/7700665.html) spreading AI-generated propaganda, to [political parties](https://aiforensics.org/work/french-elections-2024) using AI in their campaigns.

In the US, the [public remain concerned](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/09/19/concern-over-the-impact-of-ai-on-2024-presidential-campaign/) that AI will be used to produce false information in election campaigns. But AI-generated disinformation [hasn’t yet](https://www.politico.eu/newsletter/digital-bridge/we-need-to-calm-down-about-ai-and-elections/) had significant impacts on manipulating or changing [election results](https://www.turing.ac.uk/news/no-evidence-ai-disinformation-or-deepfakes-impacted-uk-french-or-european-elections-results#:~:text=AI-Enabled%20Influence%20Operations:%20Threat%20Analysis%20of%20the%202024%20UK%20and).

But while AI-generated content may not have overwhelmed our access to reliable information so far, the phrase "AI-generated" increasingly sows confusion and distrust in our democratic discourse.

> Don’t like the claims someone is making? It’s far easier to claim that the evidence they have is AI-generated than to actually have to create competing evidence yourself

Ellen Judson, Senior Investigator at Global Witness

As with "fake news" before it, claiming something is AI-generated is now a go-to tactic to attack political opponents.

Don’t like the claims someone is making? It’s far easier to claim that the evidence they have is AI-generated than to actually have to create competing evidence yourself.

In the midst of public uncertainty about AI and rapid tech advancement, it is increasingly easy to use the idea that AI manipulation could have occurred in order to muddy the waters.

This has been particularly evident around the US election campaigns. In online discussions around the campaigns, real images are being described as AI-generated, AI images are being misattributed, and images are being manipulated to appear to be AI-generated.

For instance, Kamala Harris has been frequently accused of using AI to make the crowds at her rallies seem larger.

[Social media](https://globalwitness.org/en/topics/social-media/) users have claimed that [genuine images of crowds](https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.36ED9CW) must have been AI-generated. In another case, a parody rally image which was actually AI-generated was shared,
